patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory lapses and difficulty concentrating at work, onset approximately 2 years ago
patient.history_present_illness:
Ms. Eleanor Hartmann is a 51-year-old right-handed high school mathematics teacher who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic, accompanied by her husband, for evaluation of progressive cognitive difficulties over the past two years. She was referred by her primary care physician after multiple workplace concerns led to her being placed on medical leave three months ago.

Her husband first noted subtle changes approximately two years ago: she began misplacing her keys and phone daily, a marked change from her previously meticulous habits. Over the following year, she started making uncharacteristic arithmetic errors — most notably, entering incorrect scores on student grade sheets three times in a single semester, prompting concern from the department chair. She began relying on written notes for tasks she had previously managed entirely from memory, including simple weekly grocery lists and appointment reminders. Her husband describes two episodes in which she drove to the supermarket and, on arriving, could not recall what she had gone to buy, turning around without purchasing anything.

Over the past eight months, symptoms have worsened. She now frequently forgets conversations from earlier in the day, repeating the same questions to her husband within hours. She has difficulty recalling the names of students she has taught for a full semester. She missed three scheduled parent-teacher conferences despite written reminders on her desk; on two occasions, parents waited outside her classroom while she sat unaware inside. The school principal placed her on medical leave citing safety concerns related to students.

Of note, she has a strong and striking family history: her mother developed cognitive symptoms at age 51 (the patient's current age), was formally diagnosed with dementia at 54, required full-time care by 57, and died at 60. Her mother's brother developed cognitive decline at 49 and died in a care facility at 58. Her mother's sister is currently in memory care having noticed memory problems at 53. This three-generation pattern of early-onset dementia on the maternal side has caused extreme distress to the patient and her husband, who present with considerable anxiety about the implications.

She was evaluated by her primary care physician 14 months ago, who attributed her symptoms to anxiety and increased her escitalopram from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Her mood improved modestly, but the cognitive symptoms did not, and have continued to progress. A psychiatrist she saw 8 months ago considered depression related to work stress and family history anxiety, and recommended cognitive behavioral therapy. She has completed 12 sessions of CBT with no cognitive improvement.

She explicitly acknowledges awareness of her family history and expresses her belief, shared by her husband, that she may have 'the same thing my mother had.' Both ask about genetic testing at the time of the visit. She denies hallucinations, personality change, disinhibition, language difficulty, gait problems, tremor, falls, or bladder dysfunction. No seizures. Sleep is mildly fragmented due to anxiety but no REM behavior disorder is reported.

clinical_assessment.impression: Cognitive impairment documented on a validated bedside instrument with an amnestic-predominant profile, and delayed recall that does not recover with cueing — a storage rather than a retrieval deficit, which is the pattern of Alzheimer pathology. The informant history and the loss of instrumental independence establish decline from a previous level and place the syndrome at the dementia rather than the mild threshold. This assessment is the step that makes the syndrome measurable; imaging and biomarkers then attribute it.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation reveals prominent multi-domain cognitive deficits with adequate effort (TOMM 49/50). Verbal episodic memory is severely impaired: CVLT-3 long delay free recall 2/16 (below 1st percentile), short delay 4/16, recognition discriminability 63% — indicative of a rapid-forgetting storage deficit with limited benefit from cueing. Nonverbal delayed recall (Rey Complex Figure, 5th percentile) confirms cross-modal amnesia. Confrontation naming is mildly impaired (Boston Naming Test 48/60). Verbal fluency is reduced for both semantic (12 animals/min) and phonemic (FAS 25 total) categories. Executive function is mildly impaired (Trail Making B, 18th percentile). Visuoconstructive copying and processing speed are preserved. Mood screening borderline (Geriatric Depression Scale 5/15) but does not account for the magnitude of objective memory impairment. Profile is consistent with amnestic mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment with multi-domain involvement

output.query: PSEN1 mutation autosomal dominant Alzheimer disease early onset biomarkers natural history

results.finding: In dominantly inherited AD (DIAD) due to PSEN1, PSEN2, or APP mutations, CSF Aβ42 decreases and p-tau increases approximately 10-15 years before estimated symptom onset; amyloid PET becomes positive approximately 15 years before symptoms. Mutation carriers show accelerated biomarker trajectories compared with sporadic AD.

PSEN1 mutations account for the majority of autosomal-dominant early-onset AD families; penetrance is nearly 100%. Mean age of symptom onset varies by specific variant but is typically in the late 40s to mid-50s for most PSEN1 mutations.

results.source: NIA-AA Research Framework (Jack CR et al. Alzheimers Dement 2018;14:535-562)
results.finding: Biological definition of AD requires A+ (amyloid positivity by PET or CSF Aβ42) plus T+ (elevated p-tau by CSF or tau PET). ATN staging applies regardless of clinical syndrome, including familial autosomal-dominant AD.

output.summary: Autosomal-dominant AD due to PSEN1 mutations (identified by Bateman et al. NEJM 2012 in the DIAN cohort) exhibits near-complete penetrance with symptom onset typically in the fifth decade. Biomarker changes precede symptoms by approximately 10-15 years. NIA-AA 2018 ATN framework applies equally to familial and sporadic AD.

contraindicated_actions: Do not dismiss cognitive symptoms as anxiety or work-related stress without completing objective neuropsychological testing and structural imaging — young age does not exclude AD

Do not attribute symptoms solely to depression or escitalopram use: the progressive amnestic profile with hippocampal atrophy and biomarker positivity is inconsistent with a purely psychiatric etiology
Do not disclose PSEN1 genetic results without pre-test genetic counseling for the patient and discussion of implications for at-risk family members
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in AD
Do not start memantine as monotherapy at the mild stage — memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD only
key_reasoning_points: Onset of memory impairment at age 51 with a three-generation autosomal-dominant family history of early-onset dementia (mother at 51, maternal uncle at 49, maternal aunt at 53) defines a high-penetrance genetic syndrome requiring specific genetic testing — this is not merely 'too young for Alzheimer's'

PSEN1 pathogenic variant (c.869T>C, p.Leu290Pro) confirms autosomal-dominant familial AD: PSEN1 mutations account for the majority of dominantly inherited AD and carry near-complete penetrance (Bateman 2012, DIAN cohort)

The ATN biomarker profile (A+: reduced CSF Aβ42; T+: markedly elevated p-tau 181; N+: elevated total tau; positive amyloid PET) satisfies NIA-AA 2018 biological definition of AD independently of clinical syndrome
Hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA score 2) at age 51 is highly atypical and cannot be attributed to normal aging — it is a structural correlate of established neurodegeneration

The 'too young for Alzheimer's' cognitive anchor is a common source of diagnostic delay in familial AD; early-onset autosomal-dominant AD is a well-characterized entity with symptom onset typically in the late 40s to mid-50s for many PSEN1 variants

Pre- and post-test genetic counseling is an ethical requirement before and after PSEN1 genetic disclosure — at-risk first-degree relatives (brother, children) have a 50% a priori risk and require independent counseling before predictive testing
